results.authors: CADISS trial investigators (Markus HS, Hayter E, Levi C, et al.)
results.key_finding: In 250 patients with extracranial carotid or vertebral dissection randomised within 7 days of symptom onset, stroke recurrence at 3 months was low (about 2%) and did not differ between antiplatelet and anticoagulant treatment; one major bleed (subarachnoid haemorrhage) occurred with anticoagulation.
results.title: Antiplatelet treatment compared with anticoagulation treatment for cervical artery dissection (CADISS): a randomised trial

results.authors: Engelter ST, Traenka C, Gensicke H, et al.
results.key_finding: In cervical artery dissection, aspirin did not meet the non-inferiority criterion against vitamin K antagonists for a composite of clinical and MRI outcomes; ischaemic events were few and occurred mainly in the aspirin group, major bleeding only with vitamin K antagonists.
results.title: Aspirin versus anticoagulation in cervical artery dissection (TREAT-CAD): an open-label, randomised, non-inferiority trial

results.key_finding: Cervical artery dissection causes about 2% of all ischaemic strokes and 10 to 25% of strokes in young and middle-aged adults; local signs (head or neck pain, Horner syndrome, pulsatile tinnitus) often precede ischaemia.
results.title: Cervical-artery dissections: predisposing factors, diagnosis, and outcome

output.summary: In extracranial cervical artery dissection, antiplatelet and anticoagulant treatment have not been shown to differ in stroke prevention (CADISS), and aspirin was not shown non-inferior to vitamin K antagonists in TREAT-CAD. Guidelines accept either class for at least 3 months, and follow-up vessel imaging assesses recanalization.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not attribute the episode to cluster headache or migraine: cluster headache can itself cause a partial Horner syndrome, but here the oculosympathetic signs persist as the pain eases instead of accompanying discrete attacks, this is a first single event lasting hours rather than attacks of 15 to 180 minutes, and it is accompanied by neck pain. Urgent vessel imaging is required.
Do not prescribe triptans or ergot derivatives for headache after a cervical artery dissection.
Do not combine anticoagulation with antiplatelet therapy for the dissection.
Do not discharge without antithrombotic therapy and a follow-up vessel imaging plan.
required_recommendations: Recognize painful Horner syndrome with ipsilateral retro-orbital and neck pain as a left cervical internal carotid artery dissection until proven otherwise, and confirm it with urgent vessel imaging (CTA, or MRI with fat-saturated T1 and MRA).

Start antiplatelet therapy now (for example aspirin 300 mg once, then 75 to 100 mg daily) or anticoagulation, and continue it for at least 3 months for the extracranial carotid dissection (AHA/ASA 2026 Early Secondary Prevention rec 7, COR 2a; CADISS, TREAT-CAD). No reperfusion therapy is indicated: NIHSS 0 and no infarct.

Stop sumatriptan and avoid all triptans and ergot derivatives (vasoconstrictors in a dissected carotid); stop ibuprofen (it blunts the antiplatelet effect of aspirin and adds bleeding risk); use acetaminophen for pain.
Admit for observation with serial neurological examination, because the risk of ischemic stroke is highest in the first days after dissection; any new deficit triggers an immediate stroke evaluation.
Repeat non-invasive vessel imaging (CTA or MRA) at 3 to 6 months to assess recanalization, residual stenosis or pseudoaneurysm and to decide the duration of antithrombotic therapy.

Advise and support smoking cessation; assess the LDL of 142 mg/dL by primary-prevention cardiovascular risk (the dissection itself is not a statin indication); repeat TSH with free T4 after the acute illness.

key_clinical_evidence: Painful Horner syndrome (left ptosis and miosis, anisocoria greater in dim light) with abrupt left retro-orbital and neck pain during exertion is the typical local presentation of a cervical internal carotid artery dissection and calls for urgent vessel imaging whatever the migraine history.

Facial sweating is preserved: in carotid dissection the sympathetic lesion is postganglionic along the internal carotid artery, while the sudomotor fibres to the face travel with the external carotid artery, so facial anhidrosis is absent. This localizes the Horner syndrome to the carotid and separates it from a central or preganglionic lesion.
Left-sided tinnitus since onset is a recognized local symptom of internal carotid dissection (pulsatile tinnitus) and should not be attributed to anxiety.
CT within 6 hours of the abrupt exertional pain shows no subarachnoid blood, and vessel imaging shows no aneurysm.
CTA shows an intimal flap, crescentic mural hematoma and string-sign narrowing of the left ICA from about 2 cm distal to the bifurcation to the skull base, without occlusion or pseudoaneurysm.

Three hours after onset the intramural hematoma is isointense to mildly hyperintense on fat-saturated T1; the bright methemoglobin crescent appears from about day 2 to 3, so its absence does not argue against an acute dissection.
DWI shows no infarct and the NIHSS is 0: reperfusion therapy is not a question, and management aims to prevent the ischemic stroke whose risk is highest in the first days after dissection.
Pharmacologic confirmation of the Horner syndrome is not needed once vessel imaging shows the dissection.

Extracranial carotid or vertebral dissection: antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy for at least 3 months (AHA/ASA 2026 Early Secondary Prevention rec 7, COR 2a); CADISS and TREAT-CAD showed no clear advantage of either class in extracranial dissection.
Cardiac work-up (echocardiogram, rhythm monitoring) contributes little once a dissection explains the presentation and no infarct has occurred.

metadata.difficulty_description: Moderate. Painful Horner syndrome mimics cluster headache or migraine with autonomic features; the migraine history and the tinnitus attributed to anxiety are red herrings, and incidental laboratory findings (TSH 5.2 mIU/L, LDL 142 mg/dL) add confounders. The diagnosis rests on vessel imaging: CTA shows the dissection, and MRI shows the acute intramural hematoma and the absence of infarct. The agent must recognize Horner syndrome as a localizing sign for ICA pathology rather than a primary headache feature.
metadata.difficulty_rationale: Carotid dissection with painful Horner syndrome WITHOUT completed stroke — atypical presentation requiring vessel imaging and antithrombotic prophylaxis.
metadata.revision_reason: Independent Reviewer 2 stroke audit: NCCT and CTA separated; MRI optional; CTP routed only to two extended-window cases; routine MRA/TCD/duplex duplication removed; acute labs carry explicit do-not-delay rules; EEG retained for one seizure-mimic case

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Kemal Arslan is a 41-year-old right-handed man with a history of migraine without aura and a significant smoking history who presents to the emergency department after developing sudden onset of a sharp, severe pain behind his left eye approximately three hours ago. The pain began abruptly during vigorous physical exertion and was immediately followed by the sensation that his left eyelid was 'drooping' and that his left eye appeared 'smaller' than usual. His wife confirmed that the left pupil appeared smaller and the eyelid was partially closed. The pain has since evolved into a dull, persistent ache localized behind the left eye and extending into the left side of the neck. He rates the pain as 6 out of 10 at present, down from 8 out of 10 at onset. He denies any visual changes including blurred vision, double vision, or loss of visual field. He denies any limb weakness, numbness, tingling, difficulty speaking, or difficulty swallowing. There has been no headache with aura features, photophobia, phonophobia, or nausea, and the patient states this pain is distinctly different from his usual migraines, which he describes as bilateral throbbing headaches without any eye or eyelid involvement. There was no head or neck trauma preceding the event. He did not perform any unusual neck movements or chiropractic manipulation. He has not had any recent upper respiratory tract infection. He denies any palpitations, chest pain, shortness of breath, or syncope. He has never had similar symptoms before. He has been in his usual state of health otherwise. The patient has smoked one pack of cigarettes per day for the past twenty years and uses sumatriptan occasionally for migraines. He denies illicit drug use. He drove himself to the ED against his wife's wishes, as he initially thought the symptoms were just another migraine. On further questioning, he reports mild intermittent tinnitus on the left side since the event began, which he attributes to anxiety.
